title: The Nawab of Malerkotla
hookLine: Sher Muhammad Khan protested the execution of the Sahibzade, and Sikhs have honored Malerkotla ever since

cards: Sirhind, the governor's court. Two small boys stand before Wazir Khan. The sentence is about to be spoken, and the men around the governor can see where it is going.

To object now is to take the wrong side of the man in charge, in public, with your name attached. One of the men in that court is a Muslim nobleman, a guest there, with every reason to keep quiet. He speaks instead.

teach.b: His name was Sher Muhammad Khan, the Nawab, the ruler, of a small state called Malerkotla.
Tradition says he was present at Sirhind when the governor, Wazir Khan, was deciding what to do with Zorawar Singh and Fateh Singh, the Guru's younger sons. He was not a friend of the Guru.
Tradition even says he had fought against the Guru's forces. And still, when the sentence of death was spoken, he protested.

The boys were children, he said, and children must not be punished for what their father had done. Sikhs call his protest the haa da naara, the cry of protest against injustice. Here is the hard part.
It didn't work. The governor went ahead. The boys were killed.
The Nawab could not save them. So why do Sikhs remember him with such honor? Sikh memory doesn't measure speaking up only by whether it wins.
He told the truth in a room that didn't want to hear it, at a cost to himself, for children of another faith.
Tradition says that when Guru Gobind Singh heard what the Nawab had done, he blessed him and his town, and Sikhs have honored Malerkotla ever since.

Set him beside yesterday's cook. Two people at Sirhind, a Muslim noble in the court and a cook in the kitchen, who could not change the sentence and still did not look away. One carried something warm up the stairs.
The other said, out loud, in front of the governor, that children must not be punished.

how: Sikhs remember the Nawab of Malerkotla's protest whenever the story of the Sahibzade is told, especially in the December remembrances, and speak of the town of Malerkotla with gratitude.

games.q: you're a nobleman in the governor's court. two small boys, sons of a man you've fought against, are about to be sentenced to death. what do you do?
o: keep your eyes down; it isn't your fight.
protest that children must not be punished.
games.why: Sher Muhammad Khan protested. it didn't save the boys, but Sikhs remember his cry, and the Guru, tradition says, blessed him for it.

practice: Think of a room you'll be in soon, a meeting, a family table, where someone without much power gets talked about or decided about: a new employee, a kid, someone who isn't there.
Find the one simple sentence you could say, the way the Nawab's was simple: that isn't fair, or let's hear their side. Rehearse it once, quietly, on an out-breath.

wordCard.voice: Malerkotla. The small state whose Nawab, Sher Muhammad Khan, protested in the court at Sirhind that children must not be punished, and whose town Sikhs honor for it. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: haa da naara, the cry of protest; Sikhs use it for the Nawab's protest at Sirhind.

carryVoice: Your line: he spoke up. It didn't win, and it still counts. That's the end of a week.
